set.body: worklog close and worklog update look up the item by exact dict key (fold(...).items.get(a.item) / base(a.item, ...)) instead of resolving prefixes the way worklog reopen already does (id.startswith(a.item)). Passing an 8-char prefix — the normal form worklog show/list output and the docs recommend — silently writes a new orphan phantom item under the short id instead of erroring or resolving to the real item; on update it also skips taxonomy validation since the current-state lookup silently returns {}. Reproduced live: 'worklog close 01KYA8MD' (valid prefix of 01KYA8MDY5HP9MC5KQMJX3BN84) created an orphan closed item instead of closing the real one. Fix: give close/update the same prefix-resolution + not-found error that reopen already has.

A closed item that was NEVER pushed (no external.key) and is forced into scope via --keys crashes with KeyError: 'key' instead of create-then-close. Repro: bin/worklog sync --dry-run --keys <ulid-of-closed-never-remote-item>. Hit while reconciling 01KYAH3VHPSEK2RY63J7Y109FR (release item, done, never remote) during v0.14.0 wiki/ticket publish; worked around by manually running the adapter's create step + worklog link before syncing, so the item enters the already-working closed+ext.key path. Fix: in the closed branch, if not ext.get('key'), do create-then-close (mirror the non-closed create path) instead of assuming update-then-close.

set.body: The GitHub adapter creates the issue and then makes a second call to read back its revision. If that second call is rate-limited it reports a retryable failure — but the issue already exists. The dispatcher retries the whole create up to four times, so a single rate limit can leave four duplicate issues on the board. Nothing between 'created remotely' and 'recorded locally' may fail retryably.
set.resolution: create now goes through the REST endpoint, which returns number+url+updated_at in one call, so no retryable failure can happen after the issue exists; update keeps its read-back because re-editing is idempotent. Regression: tests/test_github_adapter.py drives the adapter through a stub gh and asserts no read-back after create
set.title: GitHub adapter can file duplicate issues when rate-limited mid-create

set.body: Taking a release snapshot copies the current roadmap file as-is rather than regenerating it from the work log first. If the log has changed since the roadmap was last generated, the release freezes a picture that was already out of date -- and because snapshots are frozen, the wrong picture is permanent. It should either regenerate the roadmap itself, or refuse to run when the roadmap on disk is stale. Two releases in a row have frozen a snapshot missing the release's own work item.
set.title: roadmap-snapshot freezes whatever is on disk instead of rendering first

set.body: The generated roadmap only shows an epic when at least one of its children is still open. The moment an epic's last child closes, the epic disappears from the roadmap -- while still counting as open work everywhere else. Finished-but-unclosed epics therefore rot invisibly: one was found open three releases after its last child shipped. The roadmap should surface an epic that has no open children so someone can close it.
set.title: Roadmap hides epics whose children are all closed but which are still open

set.body: Linking now refuses a ticket another item already owns, so the only remaining way to create a duplicate is a git merge of two branches that each claimed the same ticket. Sync catches that before anything reaches the tracker, but the merge itself is the earliest possible moment to catch it, and it happens on every machine rather than only where someone runs sync.
set.title: Catch duplicate ticket ownership at merge time, not just at sync

set.body: Sync can be pointed at specific tickets to force them into the run, and that match is by ticket number. If more than one item claims that ticket, the flag drags every claimant in at once — which is exactly the reflex an operator reaches for while repairing a duplicate. It should refuse an ambiguous ticket number and say which items claim it.

set.body: Both commands take a free-text field name. Naming the field that holds an item's external ticket identity writes a plain string where the rest of the system expects a structured value, and every later sync then crashes reading it. Only fields that can legitimately disagree between local and remote should be accepted.

set.body: When the tracker reports that a ticket is gone, the adapter contract says to clear the item's link so it can be filed afresh. Sync only clears its change-detection state, so the item keeps trying to update a ticket that is not there, every run. The command to clear a link now exists — but doing it automatically on a transient error would file a duplicate, so this needs a deliberate policy first.

set.body:
The work log is compacted on a nightly schedule, and branches merge their logs by taking every line from both sides. A branch opened before a compaction and merged after it therefore restores every line the compaction removed. The recorded state is unaffected, but the size win is lost and nothing warns. Either compact after merges rather than on a timer, or skip compaction while a branch predates the cut.

Raised from P3 to P1 on 2026-07-30 after a live near-miss during routine branch cleanup. A scheduled compaction landed on main and cut the todo log from 939 lines to 22. A working copy that still held the pre-compaction log, plus two new events, was one ordinary pull away from a union merge that would have restored all 897 removed lines. Nothing in the tooling would have flagged it; the corruption was avoided only because someone compared the line counts by hand before merging. This is not a rare cross-branch edge case, it is reachable from the most common command in the repo, so it needs a guard rather than a note.
set.title: Log compaction is silently undone by any branch that spans it

set.body: After the v0.18.0 close-out, every release, publish and design-doc branch from v0.6.0 onward was fully merged into main, leaving 20 local and 84 remote branches that no longer pointed at any unmerged work. Two git worktrees were also still registered from a Claude Code session that had ended; both were clean and their branches merged. Deleted the merged branches on both sides and unregistered the stale worktrees, so the repo now shows only main locally and remotely. No commits were lost: every deleted branch was verified fully contained in origin/main first.
set.title: Prune merged branches and orphaned worktrees after v0.18.0

set.body: When an item's priority changes, sync adds the label for the new priority but never removes the label for the old one. The ticket ends up carrying both, so any filter or board column that selects on priority matches the item twice, and a reader cannot tell which value is current. Seen on 2026-07-30 when a bug was raised from P3 to P1 and the ticket came back labelled both P1 and P3. Priority is single-valued by definition, so the push should replace the whole priority label group rather than add to it. The same treatment is needed for any other single-valued field pushed as a label, level and kind included.
set.title: Priority change leaves the old priority label on the ticket

set.body: Sync refuses to push items that have no title, which is correct: they are fold debris from a mistyped or truncated item id, and pushing one would file an untitled ticket in the tracker. But it reports them as drift on every run even after they have been closed or cancelled, so two settled stubs have appeared in the drift section of every sync for weeks. One of them records its own resolution as 'orphan from id typo; neutralized, compaction sweeps it tonight', written on 2026-07-19 and still present on 2026-07-30. Drift is the section an operator is supposed to read; filling it with two lines that can never be acted on teaches people to skim it, which is how a real drift line gets missed. Report untitled debris only while it is still open.
set.title: Settled orphan debris is reported as drift on every sync run

set.body: When a union merge resurrects events a compaction removed, the pre-commit merge guard blocks the merge commit and prints: 'Run: python3 bin/compact.py .work/todo.jsonl .work/done.jsonl to recompact.' That remedy cannot be followed. compact.py refuses to run while the logs have uncommitted changes ('compaction must be its own commit, spec 7') -- and the blocked merge IS the uncommitted change. The guard prevents the commit that compaction requires, so the only ways out are --no-verify or git merge --abort, neither of which the message mentions. Hit live on 2026-07-31 when the nightly compaction landed on main while a PR was in CI. The working resolution is to abort the merge, restore the logs from the compacted branch, and re-apply the branch's own events on top of the compacted base -- same fold, far fewer lines. Either teach compact.py to accept a merge-in-progress, or change the guard's message to print the resolution that actually works.
set.resolution: Guard now names the real risk (the fold drops these on read) and points at worklog merge-rescue, which performs ADR-0005's manual resolution: keep the compacted side, re-emit this branch's own events above the watermark, verify nothing vanished. Recompaction was rejected as a remedy — it would verify against an already-lossy fold. ADR-0006 corrects ADR-0005's hygiene classification.
set.title: Merge guard's printed remedy cannot be run from the state it creates

set.body: The fold drops any event whose id sorts at or below a compaction watermark, on the assumption that the compaction already folded it into a snapshot. That assumption only holds for events the compaction actually saw. An event created on a branch before the compaction ran on main was never folded into any snapshot, yet it sorts below the watermark, so merging the branch back makes the fold discard it and the work vanishes with no error. Reproduced deterministically: an item created on a branch disappears entirely after the merge. This is the real reason the merge guard must keep blocking, and it is why recompacting during a blocked merge is unsafe -- the recompaction would verify successfully against a fold that has already discarded the branch's events, making the loss permanent. The guard currently catches every instance, so nothing is lost today, but the underlying watermark rule is unsound and fixing it properly changes how compaction records what it folded.
set.resolution: Compaction now records a per-item 'through' on each snapshot, the fold drops per item (an item with no snapshot never loses events), and a snapshot sorts at its through rather than its mint time so a branch's later close applies on top instead of being erased. ADR-0007. Legacy logs fold unchanged.
set.title: Compaction watermark can silently drop branch-local events the snapshot never folded

set.body: The commit-msg hook exempts merge commits from its item-reference rule, and the pre-commit hook only syntax-checks the event log and bin/ -- it never looks at tests/ or the plugin scripts. A merge that leaves conflict markers in those files therefore commits cleanly, and the damage is only found when someone runs the test suite. Hit twice while merging main into feature branches: markers survived in tests/test_plugin.py and in the plugin install/uninstall scripts. The fix is cheap and belongs in pre-commit, which already reads every staged file: refuse any staged text file containing a conflict marker, with no merge exemption, because a merge commit is exactly when this happens.
set.resolution: pre-commit refuses any staged file containing a conflict marker, with no merge exemption — a merge is exactly when this happens.
set.title: Conflict markers can reach a commit: the merge exemption plus unparsed tests

set.body: Two agents working in different worktrees or branches mint event ids from the same clock and pure randomness, so ids created in the same millisecond sort arbitrarily and carry nothing about where they came from. Replace five characters of a locally-generated ULID's entropy with the short git commit hash, keeping the 26-character format and the time prefix intact, so events from different branches are distinguishable and traceable at a glance. The deterministic ingest id is deliberately excluded: it must stay byte-identical across machines for the same remote change, and a per-clone git hash would break that.
set.resolution: Locally-minted ULIDs carry the 5-char short git hash in place of 5 chars of entropy; 26-char format, time prefix and sort order unchanged. deterministic() deliberately excluded so ingest ids stay byte-identical across clones.
set.title: Stamp generated ULIDs with the short git hash so concurrent branches diverge

set.body: v0.19.0 stamped the short git hash into locally-minted ULIDs by overwriting five characters of entropy. That was the wrong trade: an id is issued once and must never collide, so spending entropy to carry provenance weakens the one guarantee the id exists to provide. Restore the full 80 bits and record the originating git commit as a separate property on every event instead, which also traces better -- an item's ULID is minted once, so it could only ever name the branch the item was created on, while a per-event field names the origin of every event.
set.resolution: ULIDs are back to full 80-bit entropy; the git short sha now rides on every event as its own 'git' field. Provenance is per-event rather than baked into an id that is minted once, so a later update names the commit it was actually authored at.

set.body: When a compaction lands mid-branch, the rescue re-emits the branch's own events with fresh identifiers so the snapshot cannot overwrite them. Those identifiers sort by time, so a re-emitted early event lands above a later event that was not re-emitted, and the older state wins. Observed on the Codex packaging branch: an item that read done before the merge read in_progress after it, with no warning and no lost events. The rescue should re-emit an item's whole surviving history in its original order, or refuse to re-emit an event older than one it is leaving in place.
set.resolution: Fixed with a regression test.

set.body: A weekly report counts an item as shipped only when a close event falls inside the window. Compaction folds an item's events into a single snapshot, so the close event no longer exists and the item silently drops out of the report even though it closed inside the window. The close time is not lost: the snapshot's watermark is the last event it folded, which for a closed item is the close itself.

set.body:
The Stop hook, hooks/stop-worklog-check.sh, runs every git command as 'git -C "$PWD"' and never calls 'git worktree list'. It asks two questions in one checkout: is the tree dirty outside .work/ and docs/roadmap.md, and is .work/todo.jsonl unchanged versus HEAD. If dirty is yes and the log is unchanged it concludes unrecorded work and blocks.

Worklog policy tells concurrent sessions to use a git worktree. Linked worktrees share one object store but each has its own working tree, its own branch, and its own .work/todo.jsonl. So the hook's two questions get answered by a checkout that is not the one the agent wrote to.

The false block: the session opens on the primary checkout, the agent records everything in a linked worktree, and the primary tree happens to be dirty for an unrelated reason. The hook sees dirty plus an unchanged primary log and blocks, though the work is fully recorded next door. The inverse also holds: a clean, fully logged worktree cannot satisfy a hook that never opens it. Copying events between trees by hand is forbidden, so there is no supported way to make the hook see the other log. The recommended concurrency model and the Stop check are at odds.

Fix: keep the dirty check at $PWD as the signal that work happened, but before blocking, walk 'git worktree list' and allow the stop if any checkout in the repo holds an uncommitted change to .work/todo.jsonl.

Known gap this fix does not close: the hook's proof of recording is an UNCOMMITTED change to todo.jsonl, so a session that records and then commits its items still reads as unrecorded. That gap exists in the single-checkout case too and needs a session-start marker to fix. Track it separately.
set.title: Stop hook accuses a correctly-logged worktree session of skipping the log
